**Introduction********** Cedar Springs is a compact city located in Kent County, Michigan, about 20 miles north of downtown Grand Rapids. Incorporated as a city in 1959, Cedar Springs originated as a lumber town and has maintained its small‑town charm. The city covers roughly two square miles and continues to attract residents seeking affordable living within reach of metropolitan employment.
**Lifestyle and Entertainment********** Life in Cedar Springs is centered on community connection, outdoor recreation, and small‑town charm. The White Pine Trail State Park provides a long recreational path for biking, running, and snowmobiling, cutting right through the city. Annual traditions like the Red Flannel Festival foster strong community ties, and residents enjoy quiet evenings, local eateries, and family‑friendly amenities.
**Climate and Weather********** Cedar Springs has a humid continental climate, with warm summers and cold, snowy winters. Average highs reach the low 80s in July, while January lows often drop below 20°F. Snowfall is significant due to proximity to Lake Michigan, contributing to long winters but also supporting winter sports and scenic snowy landscapes.
**Education System********** The Cedar Springs Public Schools district serves students from elementary through high school. The system emphasizes community involvement and offers extracurriculars and athletic programs. While academic metrics vary by grade level, the district is recognized for a supportive learning environment. The nearest higher education institutions are located in Grand Rapids, offering nearby college and vocational opportunities.
**Demographics********** Cedar Springs has a population of roughly 3,660 residents. The median age is approximately 39 years. The population is predominantly White, with small but growing racial and ethnic diversity. Median household income is around $56,700, and the homeownership rate stands near 60 percent. Many residents are young families, professionals, or retirees drawn to the balance of cost, safety, and community.
**Crime Rate and Safety********** The crime rate in Cedar Springs is generally low, with most incidents related to property crimes such as theft or vandalism. Violent crime is rare. A dedicated local police department, strong community participation, and neighborhood cohesion contribute to a sense of safety and civic pride.

**Cost of Living********** Cedar Springs offers a cost of living lower than the national average. Housing is notably affordable, with median home values around $200,000. Utilities, groceries, and transportation costs fall within or below typical benchmarks. The city provides an appealing cost structure for first‑time homeowners, young families, and those looking to stretch their dollars while remaining near Grand Rapids.
**Economy and Employment********** Many residents commute to Grand Rapids or other nearby towns for employment. Key sectors include light manufacturing, education, health services, construction, and local government. The downtown core is revitalizing with more small businesses, service shops, and eateries. Local economic development efforts continue to prioritize housing and infrastructure.
**Culture and History********** Cedar Springs has roots dating back to the mid‑1800s as a logging and lumber town. The name derives from the abundance of cedar trees and natural springs in the area. The city honors its history through preserved architecture, local museums, and annual festivals like the Red Flannel Festival, which dates to 1939 and continues to be a cornerstone of local identity.
**Public Transit System********** Public transportation is limited in Cedar Springs, with most residents relying on private vehicles. The city is connected via U.S. Route 131, offering direct access to Grand Rapids and surrounding areas. There is no local light rail or fixed‑route bus service, although regional ride‑share and carpooling options exist for commuters.

Cedar Springs is located just 20 minutes north of Michigan’s second largest city, Grand Rapids. Situated in northern Kent County, Cedar Springs covers about 2.1 square miles and has a population of 3,509. The community was named for the fine springs bordered by a grove of Cedar trees. Less than a mile from US 131, Cedar Springs provides easy access to the cultural amenities of the greater Grand Rapids area. Cedar Springs is an attractive community with tree-lined streets and a varied housing base. Taxes in Cedar Springs have remained steady with the City millage rate of 15.0642.
Cedar Springs has a small retail business district and a stable industrial base. The community has vast possibilities for future growth. Significant industry and business have been attracted to the Cedar Springs area, including Display Pack and various precision tool and die companies.
Cedar Springs is part of the Cedar Springs Public School district, which encompasses 110 square miles and is comprised of the City of Cedar Springs and 7 surrounding townships. Cedar Springs Public Schools are located on a single 100 acre campus near downtown Cedar Springs. The school system has recently completed a $27 million building and renovation project.
The Cedar Springs Area Parks and Recreation Board is actively exploring new means to provide programs for youth and adults. The annual Red Flannel Festival was first celebrated in 1939, making it one of the oldest festivals in Michigan. Red Flannel Day takes place on the first Saturday in October to celebrate the famous “drop seat” red long johns and red flannel nightwear.
Overall, Cedar Springs is a desirable residential community with its own identity and charm. The City has all of the benefits of a small community, while simultaneously offering big city amenities.

### High Quality of Life Throughout the County
Kent County is the fourth largest population center in Michigan. Covering 856 square miles, the County is home to 596,666 people. The County is composed of 21 townships, five villages and nine cities.
The greater Grand Rapids area forms the urban center of the County. Grand Rapids is known as the home of the 38th President of the United States, Gerald R. Ford. The Gerald R. Ford Museum is located in the City of Grand Rapids and the Gerald R. Ford International Airport is located within Kent County.
Kent County is the economic and manufacturing center of West Michigan. Major employers include Spectrum Health, Meijer Incorporated, Steelcase Incorporated, Alticor Incorporated and Spartan Stores. It is also the home of the Frederik Meijer Gardens, a significant cultural landmark of the Midwest.
Kent County offers a thriving arts community and a diverse range of entertainment options for every season. The County has over 50 parks, offering activities such as golfing, swimming, biking, roller blading, walking, cross country skiing, fishing, boating, camping and a variety of playing fields. The award-winning 12,000 seat Van Andel Arena, located in Grand Rapids, is home to the Griffins hockey team and the Rampage arena football team, as well as major concerts and sporting events. The Michigan White Caps call Fifth Third Ballpark their home. All of these venues are located within an easy 15-20 minute drive from Cedar Springs.

**Kent County** is located in the U.S. state of Michigan. As of the 2020 Census, the county had a population of 657,974,[[2]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kent_County,_Michigan#cite_note-QF-2) making it the fourth most populous county in Michigan, and the largest outside of the Detroit area. Its county seat and largest city is Grand Rapids, Michigan’s second largest city.[[3]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kent_County,_Michigan#cite_note-GR6-3) The county was set off in 1831, and organized in 1836.[[1]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kent_County,_Michigan#cite_note-clarke-1) It is named for New York jurist and legal scholar James Kent,[[4]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kent_County,_Michigan#cite_note-4) who represented the Michigan Territory in its dispute with Ohio over the Toledo Strip.
Kent County is part of the Grand Rapids metropolitan area and is West Michigan's economic and manufacturing center. It is home of the Frederik Meijer Gardens, a significant cultural landmark of the Midwest. The Gerald R. Ford International Airport is the county's primary location for regional and international airline traffic.

The Grand River runs through the county. On its west bank are burial mounds, remnants of the Hopewell Indians who lived there.[[5]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kent_County,_Michigan#cite_note-5) In the 18th century the Odawa migrated to this area and established multiple villages along the Grand River valley.[[6]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kent_County,_Michigan#cite_note-HISTORY1881-6) By the 19th century there were estimated to be over 1000 Odawa.[[6]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kent_County,_Michigan#cite_note-HISTORY1881-6)[[7]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kent_County,_Michigan#cite_note-WILD-7) The fur trade became an important industry in the valley during the early 19th century. After the War of 1812, Rix Robinson and Louis Campau were the earliest traders in the area.[[8]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kent_County,_Michigan#cite_note-8) In 1826, Campau established a trading post in Grand Rapids. In 1831, he bought land and platted the town. Campau is considered the town's "father".[[9]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kent_County,_Michigan#cite_note-HISTORY1870-9)[[10]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kent_County,_Michigan#cite_note-Fued-10)[[11]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kent_County,_Michigan#cite_note-Statues-11) One year later, government surveyor Lucius Lyon purchased land north of Campau's property.

Campau surveyed and platted the village following Native American trails[[10]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kent_County,_Michigan#cite_note-Fued-10) and Lyon had platted his property in an English grid format, which meant there were two adjoining villages, with different platting formats.[[10]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kent_County,_Michigan#cite_note-Fued-10) Campau later merged the villages under the name of Grand Rapids.[[10]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kent_County,_Michigan#cite_note-Fued-10)
In 1831, it was set off from Kalamazoo County.[[12]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kent_County,_Michigan#cite_note-12) In 1838, Grand Rapids was incorporated[[10]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kent_County,_Michigan#cite_note-Fued-10) as the county's first village. By the end of the century, stimulated by the construction of several sawmills, the area was a significant center for agriculture, logging, and manufacturing furniture.
Rockford Dam in Rockford, Michigan
According to the U.S. Census Bureau, the county has an area of 872 square miles (2,260 km 2), of which 847 square miles (2,190 km 2) is land and 25 square miles (65 km 2) (2.9%) is water.[[13]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kent_County,_Michigan#cite_note-GR1-13) Kent County's highest point is Fisk Knob Park,[[14]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kent_County,_Michigan#cite_note-Fisk_Knob-14) in Solon Township, at 1048 feet.[[15]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kent_County,_Michigan#cite_note-Fisk_Knob_Elevation-15)

*   Grand River, flows through the county from its eastern border to the west, and after passing through Ottawa County, empties into Lake Michigan at Grand Haven. It has three tributaries in Kent County, listed in order of convergence:  
*   Flat River, enters the county from the east, and joins the Grand from the north, in Lowell.  
*   Thornapple River, enters the county from the south, and joins the Grand in Ada.  
*   Rogue River, enters the county from the north, and joins the Grand in Belmont.
These hiking and biking trails run through the county:
*   North Country Trail, runs north–south the length of the county, passing through Cedar Springs, Grattan and Lowell. Lowell is the trail's half-way point, and the national headquarters of the North Country Trail Association is located here.  
*   Thornapple Trail, begins in Kentwood and runs southeast through Dutton and Caledonia.  
*   White Pine Trail begins in Comstock Park and runs northeast through Belmont, Rockford, Cedar Springs, and Sand Lake.  
*   Kent Trails (which is singular in spite of the 's') runs north–south from John Ball Park in Grand Rapids to 84th Street in Byron Township, with an extension that runs east/west along 76th Street and north–south from 76th Street to Douglas Walker Park on 84th street.  
*   The Frederik Meijer Trail, which, as of November 2008, was incomplete, runs east/west mostly along the M-6 freeway and will connect the Kent Trails and the Thornapple Trail when completed.  
*   Cannon Township Trail runs through Cannon Township in the eastern part of the county from Cannon Township Center on M-44. It runs along M-44 then south near Sunfish Lake Road, turning east through the Cannonsburg Cemetery, and ends at Warren Townsend Park near Cannonsburg.

## Places worth seeing
*   ### Frederik Meijer Gardens & Sculpture Park
158 acres of gardens, a tropical conservatory, and one of the world's most-visited sculpture collections, plus a summer outdoor concert series locals plan around.
*   ### Gerald R. Ford Presidential Museum
The presidential museum and burial site of Grand Rapids' own Gerald R. Ford, on the west bank of the Grand River downtown.
*   ### John Ball Zoo
A hillside zoo on Fulton Street with animals from around the world, a zipline and ropes course, and seasonal events like Twilight Tours.
*   ### Grand Rapids Public Museum
Three floors of West Michigan history and science on the river, home to a working 1928 carousel and a planetarium.
*   ### Grand Rapids Art Museum (GRAM)
The downtown art museum on Monroe Center: rotating exhibitions, a strong design collection, and the world's first LEED Gold certified art museum building.
*   ### Blandford Nature Center
264 acres of trails, wildlife education, and a working farm on the city's northwest side, a favorite for families year-round.
*   ### Fallasburg Park & Covered Bridge
An 1871 covered bridge over the Flat River near Lowell, one of Michigan's last covered bridges still open to car traffic, inside a 336-acre county park.

## Things to do year-round
*   ### ArtPrize
The international art competition that takes over downtown Grand Rapids every fall: hundreds of venues, free to walk, nearly a million visitors. It runs for about two weeks starting in mid-September.
*   ### Beer City Ale Trail
Grand Rapids has been voted Beer City USA repeatedly for a reason: 35+ craft breweries on one trail, with a passport app that earns you free gear for checking in.
*   ### Fulton Street Farmers Market
The area's oldest farmers market, running since 1922: produce, meat, baked goods, and art from West Michigan growers and makers.
*   ### Millennium Park
One of the nation's largest urban parks: 1,400 acres across Walker, Grand Rapids, Grandville, and Wyoming with a six-acre beach, splashpad, boat rentals, and 18 miles of trails.
*   ### Fred Meijer White Pine Trail
A 92-mile paved rail-trail that starts in Comstock Park and runs north through Rockford and Cedar Springs all the way to Cadillac. Bike, run, or ski it.
*   ### West Michigan Whitecaps at LMCU Ballpark
Minor-league baseball in Comstock Park all summer: cheap seats, famous ballpark food, and Friday fireworks. The Whitecaps are the Tigers' High-A affiliate.
*   ### Grand Rapids Griffins hockey
The AHL affiliate of the Detroit Red Wings plays October through spring at Van Andel Arena downtown, a legitimately loud building on weekend nights.
*   ### Cannonsburg Ski Area
Kent County's home hill in Belmont: skiing, snowboarding, and tubing 20 minutes from downtown, with mountain biking in the summer.
*   ### Downtown Rockford & the Rogue River
A classic river-town main street on the White Pine Trail: shops, restaurants, the dam overlook, and salmon runs in the fall.

## Moving to Kent County: common questions
How do property taxes work in Kent County?  
You'll get two bills a year: a summer bill issued around July 1 (the larger of the two) and a winter bill around December 1, both from your city or township treasurer. If the home is your primary residence, make sure the Principal Residence Exemption is on file; it exempts you from up to 18 mills of school operating tax. If your mortgage escrows taxes, your servicer pays the bills, but the PRE filing is still on you. Your bills will often rise the year after you buy: Michigan caps how fast taxable value can grow (inflation or 5%, whichever is less) only while one owner holds the home, and under MCL 211.27a the taxable value uncaps to the state equalized value in the calendar year after a sale, so the seller's tax bill is not a guide to yours. If you buy in Grand Rapids or Walker, budget for a city income tax as well; the next question covers it.
Do Grand Rapids and Walker have a city income tax?  
Yes. Both are on the Michigan Department of Treasury's list of the 24 cities that levy one. **Kent County** is located in the U.S. state of Michigan. As of the 2020 Census, the county had a population of 657,974,[[2]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kent_County,_Michigan#cite_note-QF-2) making it the fourth most populous county in Michigan, and the largest outside of the Detroit area. Its county seat and largest city is Grand Rapids, Michigan’s second largest city.[[3]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kent_County,_Michigan#cite_note-GR6-3) The county was set off in 1831, and organized in 1836.[[1]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kent_County,_Michigan#cite_note-clarke-1) It is named for New York jurist and legal scholar James Kent,[[4]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kent_County,_Michigan#cite_note-4) who represented the Michigan Territory in its dispute with Ohio over the Toledo Strip.
Kent County is part of the Grand Rapids metropolitan area and is West Michigan's economic and manufacturing center. It is home of the Frederik Meijer Gardens, a significant cultural landmark of the Midwest. The Gerald R. Ford International Airport is the county's primary location for regional and international airline traffic.
texts.2: The Grand River runs through the county. On its west bank are burial mounds, remnants of the Hopewell Indians who lived there.[[5]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kent_County,_Michigan#cite_note-5) In the 18th century the Odawa migrated to this area and established multiple villages along the Grand River valley.[[6]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kent_County,_Michigan#cite_note-HISTORY1881-6) By the 19th century there were estimated to be over 1000 Odawa.[[6]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kent_County,_Michigan#cite_note-HISTORY1881-6)[[7]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kent_County,_Michigan#cite_note-WILD-7) The fur trade became an important industry in the valley during the early 19th century. After the War of 1812, Rix Robinson and Louis Campau were the earliest traders in the area.[[8]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kent_County,_Michigan#cite_note-8) In 1826, Campau established a trading post in Grand Rapids. In 1831, he bought land and platted the town. Campau is considered the town's "father".[[9]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kent_County,_Michigan#cite_note-HISTORY1870-9)[[10]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kent_County,_Michigan#cite_note-Fued-10)[[11]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kent_County,_Michigan#cite_note-Statues-11) One year later, government surveyor Lucius Lyon purchased land north of Campau's property.
texts.3:
Campau surveyed and platted the village following Native American trails[[10]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kent_County,_Michigan#cite_note-Fued-10) and Lyon had platted his property in an English grid format, which meant there were two adjoining villages, with different platting formats.[[10]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kent_County,_Michigan#cite_note-Fued-10) Campau later merged the villages under the name of Grand Rapids.[[10]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kent_County,_Michigan#cite_note-Fued-10)
In 1831, it was set off from Kalamazoo County.[[12]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kent_County,_Michigan#cite_note-12) In 1838, Grand Rapids was incorporated[[10]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kent_County,_Michigan#cite_note-Fued-10) as the county's first village. By the end of the century, stimulated by the construction of several sawmills, the area was a significant center for agriculture, logging, and manufacturing furniture.

According to the U.S. Census Bureau, the county has an area of 872 square miles (2,260 km 2), of which 847 square miles (2,190 km 2) is land and 25 square miles (65 km 2) (2.9%) is water.[[13]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kent_County,_Michigan#cite_note-GR1-13) Kent County's highest point is Fisk Knob Park,[[14]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kent_County,_Michigan#cite_note-Fisk_Knob-14) in Solon Township, at 1048 feet.[[15]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kent_County,_Michigan#cite_note-Fisk_Knob_Elevation-15)

*   Flat River, enters the county from the east, and joins the Grand from the north, in Lowell.  
*   Thornapple River, enters the county from the south, and joins the Grand in Ada.  
*   Rogue River, enters the county from the north, and joins the Grand in Belmont.
These hiking and biking trails run through the county:
*   North Country Trail, runs north–south the length of the county, passing through Cedar Springs, Grattan and Lowell. Lowell is the trail's half-way point, and the national headquarters of the North Country Trail Association is located here.

If the home is your primary residence, make sure the Principal Residence Exemption is on file; it exempts you from up to 18 mills of school operating tax. If your mortgage escrows taxes, your servicer pays the bills, but the PRE filing is still on you. Your bills will often rise the year after you buy: Michigan caps how fast taxable value can grow (inflation or 5%, whichever is less) only while one owner holds the home, and under MCL 211.27a the taxable value uncaps to the state equalized value in the calendar year after a sale, so the seller's tax bill is not a guide to yours. If you buy in Grand Rapids or Walker, budget for a city income tax as well; the next question covers it.
Do Grand Rapids and Walker have a city income tax?  
Yes. Both are on the Michigan Department of Treasury's list of the 24 cities that levy one. Grand Rapids taxes residents at 1.5% and nonresidents who work in the city at 0.75% of what they earn there; its Income Tax Help Center is at (616) 456-3415. Walker's city income tax is 1% for residents and 0.5% for nonresidents who work in Walker; its Income Tax Department is at (616) 791-6880. Returns for both cities are due April 30, and in the year you move in or out you would file as a part-year resident. Wyoming, Kentwood, Grandville and Kent County's other cities do not levy one, and townships and villages cannot.

## Moving to Kent County: common questions
What is the Michigan Principal Residence Exemption and when do I file it?  
The PRE (Form 2368) tells your assessor the home is your primary residence, exempting it from up to 18 mills of local school operating tax. File with your city or township assessor by June 1 to have it apply to that year's summer tax bill, or by November 1 for the winter bill. It's commonly filed as part of closing paperwork, but confirm with the assessor that it was actually recorded, because a missed PRE is one of the most common (and expensive) new-homeowner surprises in Michigan.
What order should I set up utilities in?  
Start with electric (Consumers Energy) and gas (DTE) about a week before closing; both transfer online in minutes. Water and sewer come next: in Grand Rapids call 311 to move the account, and in Wyoming, Kentwood, or East Grand Rapids contact that city's utility office. Internet installs can have a lead time of a week or more, so book that early; trash service can wait until you're in.
Does Kent County require a well and septic inspection when a home sells?  
No. Kent County has no countywide rule requiring a well or septic evaluation before a home changes hands. That is worth knowing because it is not the rule everywhere in West Michigan: Ottawa County next door has required an evaluation before transfer since 1984. Most homes in Grand Rapids and the ring suburbs are on city water and sewer anyway, but plenty of outlying townships are on a private well and septic system. If yours is one of them, pay for an evaluation during your inspection period. A septic field and a well are among the few things a standard home inspection does not cover, and a failed field is a five-figure surprise.
Am I required to shovel my sidewalk in the winter?  
In the City of Grand Rapids, yes: the ordinance gives you 24 hours after the snow stops to clear your sidewalks, and the city can charge a $95 administrative fee plus labor if it has to clear them for you after notice. Most other Kent County cities have similar rules with different clocks, so check your own city's ordinance. A good snow blower is a legitimate West Michigan homeownership expense; the county averages 70+ inches a year.

## Moving to Kent County: common questions
When is the best time to buy a home in West Michigan?  
Inventory peaks from April through early summer, which means the most choice but also the most competition; well-priced Kent County homes routinely draw multiple offers in spring. Late fall and winter bring fewer listings but more negotiating room and faster closings. Grand Rapids consistently ranks among the tighter housing markets in the country, so being pre-approved before you shop matters more here than timing the season.
Where do I go for county-level services?  
Almost everything routes through kentcountymi.gov: the County Clerk for records like deeds and vital documents, the Treasurer for delinquent taxes and dog licenses, and Kent County Parks for the parks system. For city-level issues in Grand Rapids (water, trash, sidewalks, street trees), dial 311 inside the city or (616) 456-3000. Your city or township hall handles assessing, current-year tax bills, and voter precincts.

**Kent County** is located in the U.S. state of Michigan. As of the 2020 Census, the county had a population of 657,974,[[2]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kent_County,_Michigan#cite_note-QF-2) making it the fourth most populous county in Michigan, and the largest outside of the Detroit area. Its county seat and largest city is Grand Rapids, Michigan’s second largest city.[[3]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kent_County,_Michigan#cite_note-GR6-3) The county was set off in 1831, and organized in 1836.[[1]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kent_County,_Michigan#cite_note-clarke-1) It is named for New York jurist and legal scholar James Kent,[[4]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kent_County,_Michigan#cite_note-4) who represented the Michigan Territory in its dispute with Ohio over the Toledo Strip.
Kent County is part of the Grand Rapids metropolitan area and is West Michigan's economic and manufacturing center. It is home of the Frederik Meijer Gardens, a significant cultural landmark of the Midwest. The Gerald R. Ford International Airport is the county's primary location for regional and international airline traffic.

The Grand River runs through the county. On its west bank are burial mounds, remnants of the Hopewell Indians who lived there.[[5]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kent_County,_Michigan#cite_note-5) In the 18th century the Odawa migrated to this area and established multiple villages along the Grand River valley.[[6]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kent_County,_Michigan#cite_note-HISTORY1881-6) By the 19th century there were estimated to be over 1000 Odawa.[[6]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kent_County,_Michigan#cite_note-HISTORY1881-6)[[7]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kent_County,_Michigan#cite_note-WILD-7) The fur trade became an important industry in the valley during the early 19th century. After the War of 1812, Rix Robinson and Louis Campau were the earliest traders in the area.[[8]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kent_County,_Michigan#cite_note-8) In 1826, Campau established a trading post in Grand Rapids. In 1831, he bought land and platted the town. Campau is considered the town's "father".[[9]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kent_County,_Michigan#cite_note-HISTORY1870-9)[[10]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kent_County,_Michigan#cite_note-Fued-10)[[11]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kent_County,_Michigan#cite_note-Statues-11) One year later, government surveyor Lucius Lyon purchased land north of Campau's property.

Campau surveyed and platted the village following Native American trails[[10]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kent_County,_Michigan#cite_note-Fued-10) and Lyon had platted his property in an English grid format, which meant there were two adjoining villages, with different platting formats.[[10]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kent_County,_Michigan#cite_note-Fued-10) Campau later merged the villages under the name of Grand Rapids.[[10]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kent_County,_Michigan#cite_note-Fued-10)
In 1831, it was set off from Kalamazoo County.[[12]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kent_County,_Michigan#cite_note-12) In 1838, Grand Rapids was incorporated[[10]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kent_County,_Michigan#cite_note-Fued-10) as the county's first village. By the end of the century, stimulated by the construction of several sawmills, the area was a significant center for agriculture, logging, and manufacturing furniture.

According to the U.S. Census Bureau, the county has an area of 872 square miles (2,260 km 2), of which 847 square miles (2,190 km 2) is land and 25 square miles (65 km 2) (2.9%) is water.[[13]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kent_County,_Michigan#cite_note-GR1-13) Kent County's highest point is Fisk Knob Park,[[14]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kent_County,_Michigan#cite_note-Fisk_Knob-14) in Solon Township, at 1048 feet.[[15]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kent_County,_Michigan#cite_note-Fisk_Knob_Elevation-15)

*   Grand River, flows through the county from its eastern border to the west, and after passing through Ottawa County, empties into Lake Michigan at Grand Haven. It has three tributaries in Kent County, listed in order of convergence:  
*   Flat River, enters the county from the east, and joins the Grand from the north, in Lowell.  
*   Thornapple River, enters the county from the south, and joins the Grand in Ada.  
*   Rogue River, enters the county from the north, and joins the Grand in Belmont.
These hiking and biking trails run through the county:
*   North Country Trail, runs north–south the length of the county, passing through Cedar Springs, Grattan and Lowell. Lowell is the trail's half-way point, and the national headquarters of the North Country Trail Association is located here.  
*   Thornapple Trail, begins in Kentwood and runs southeast through Dutton and Caledonia.  
*   White Pine Trail begins in Comstock Park and runs northeast through Belmont, Rockford, Cedar Springs, and Sand Lake.  
*   Kent Trails (which is singular in spite of the 's') runs north–south from John Ball Park in Grand Rapids to 84th Street in Byron Township, with an extension that runs east/west along 76th Street and north–south from 76th Street to Douglas Walker Park on 84th street.  
*   The Frederik Meijer Trail, which, as of November 2008, was incomplete, runs east/west mostly along the M-6 freeway and will connect the Kent Trails and the Thornapple Trail when completed.  
*   Cannon Township Trail runs through Cannon Township in the eastern part of the county from Cannon Township Center on M-44. It runs along M-44 then south near Sunfish Lake Road, turning east through the Cannonsburg Cemetery, and ends at Warren Townsend Park near Cannonsburg.
